description:
Black-bellied Whistling Duck (Dendrocygna autumnalis)

9 April 2016
Centennial Park
Irving, Texas

We attended an event at the South Irving Public Library which is located next to the center of Centennial Park. Afterwards we walked the site and when leaving there was a small flock of four ducks flying over Delaware Creek (originally named Indian Run Creek by the first White settlers in the late 1840s) headed our way. We didn't know what kind of ducks these were but the last three pics we took on this date were of these ducks as they flew over the creek at a fast clip to our immediate left. Only when we had the chance to view the images (and admittedly the ISO needed to have been set faster on our camera to produce a better quality image), did we notice that these were Black-bellied Whistling Ducks. This is our first observation in the field of this duck in the North Texas region. These ducks have been extending their range northward in the United States. There's enough of the image present to make the ID possible. Thanks in advance.

Here's the thumbnail sketch from All About Birds for this duck: "The Black-bellied Whistling-Duck is a boisterous duck with a brilliant pink bill and an unusual, long-legged silhouette. In places like Texas and Louisiana, watch for noisy flocks of these gaudy ducks dropping into fields to forage on seeds, or loafing on golf course ponds. Listen for them, too—these ducks really do have a whistle for their call. Common south of the U.S., Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks occur in several southern states and are expanding northward." Black-bellied Whistling Duck is an authentic resident of North America and the Western Hemisphere. Centennial Park is administered by the City of Irving, Texas.

Source: "Black-bellied Whistling Duck," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Cornell University, photographs, range map, description, resources, accessed 4.11.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Black-bellied_Whistling-Duck/id

description: These ducks were seen at Ragan Park, a municipal park located near Ybor City in a Tampa, Fl neighborhood. In the center of the park there is a shallow pond wherein a large dry dirt island has formed in the middle due to drought. These ducks were seen flocking in groups of 12-15 around other groups that totaled ~50 organisms. They were ~45cm tall when standing with necks that were ~15cm long and body lengths (beak tip to tail tip) of ~38cm. Most noticeable about these birds were their bright orange duck-like beaks, light orange webbed feet and dark brown stripe of slightly longer feathers cascading from the top of their heads to the base of their flight muscles. They walked slowly and in lines. Some foraged by submerging their heads beneath the water, some slept on one foot with their heads tucked beneath a wing on top of their backs and some stood still. They did not appear to preen and flew low and clumsily from the water and water’s edge. Some tucked their feet while flying while others let their feet dangle. They did not appear to be sexually dimorphic, however some had slightly more light grey on the lower edge of their tucked wings than others. Their bellies were dark brown to black in coloration and the majority of their back, neck, wing and face feathers were medium brown at rest. Only when the wings were extended could I see many white feathers with black tips. No ducklings were present. These birds had a high-pitch, quick, whistle-like call similar to a song bird and did not clapper their beaks much.

description:
Visual Description: These ducks had black bellies. Their feathers were a mix of brown and white and these colors led up to the neck. The neck and head were a light gray with a brown patch on top. They had black eyes with a white ring around their eyes that made them pop. The beak was a bright and vibrant orange. They were about 1-2 feet long and had a long neck. Their feet (not pictured) matched their beak.

Defining characteristics: All of the visual description provided is a defining characteristic. These species are known for their magnificent patterns with a completely black underside and orange beaks. The ring around the eye is also a key charactistic. They are noisy hence them being called "whistling ducks"

Habitat: These ducks were found in the middle of a wetland. The area was moist, tropical, and rich in nutrients. They fed on some of the aquatic leaves in the water. These ducks are found along the gulf and southern portions of Mississippi and the Atlantic, however they migrate out of the US when fall hits. 

Reference: https://www.fws.gov/southeast/wildlife/birds/black-bellied-whistling-duck/

description:
Chordata, Aves, Anseriformes, Anatidae, Dendrocygna, autumnalis. 
or the Black-bellied Whistling Duck

DESCRIPTION
Visual: Relatively small compared to other mature aged ducks roughly a foot in height and length and less than that in width. Some key features of this organism is its bright pink beak compared to its body and a unique black stripe up the back of their heads that resemble little human buzzcuts which I have never observed in nature before. These ducks also have a white stripe following along on their wings and a black underbelly, hence the common name. Though I was unable to record any sound, these organisms have a distinct sound that is quite different than a typical duck "quack" and is more similar to a bird "chirp"

Habitat: These ducks were found in their typical habitat which is marshlands along bodies of water, they are more commonly found in Brazil and only coastal waters in Mexico, they can also be found in many other coastal wet areas like the Gulf Coast and many different areas of Florida. These ducks are considered "Least concerned" on the endangered species list and in growing population, inferring they shouldn't be a very rare observation.

References:
Info on habitat
https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Black-bellied_Whistling-Duck/overview
Info on population
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-bellied_whistling_duck#Description

My first time seeing them in Everglades National Park!

Here with my former student Ryan G on a little Everglades romp. We 
hiked down the Gate 2A trail in Long Pine Key, after poking around HID 2020 near the big sinkholes. Then drove down to the end of Research Road and hiked a bit west before going to the Royal Palm area and walking the Anhinga boardwalk trail. Some highlights included seeing a common nighthawk on its nest (I accidentally flushed it). description:
aka "Lucky"

We raised this one from two-day-old chick with two other siblings when they became orphaned and ran into our house/lanai in Labor Day 2022, and didn't leave.  They mostly stayed in our lanai outside and swam in the pool.  Their parents never showed, so we did our duty.  When they finally could fly that December we released them back into the wild where they have successfully reintegrated with their congeners. Two of them return to the feeding station regularly, but have periods of days/weeks of absence.  Lucky's sister has already been impregnated by one of their amigos and all three are doing well.  As far as we are aware, we are among the very few, if any others, to raise this species to adulthood successfully.

description: On my way north to San Antonio from the Valley, I stopped at this park in San Diego -- this is a GREAT park, and I hope I remember to do some blacklighting here in the future.
Perched in Live Oak at Sunset, flew toward lagoon

Colt Creek butterfly count with Linda Cooper, Rob Epstein, and Delia Smith in our party. There were three other parties. We drove mostly unpaved roads in the southern portion of the state park, east to its boundary at the powerline cut (the state park is much larger than I realized; at nearly 6,000 acres!). The weather at the start was sunny and 77 degrees ("feels like" 77) with a light breeze. Deer Flies, mosquitoes, and humidity were non-existent. Owing to the drought, butterfly numbers were mostly low, but we had fairly high diversity (35 species for our party). Multiple records of the same species, especially Southern Skipperling (7 records, plus 22 records of 7 other skipper species) and Carolina Satyr (15 records), represent different individuals. We left at 1602, when the weather was sunny and 90 degrees ("feels like" 90), with a light breeze.

description: With Valeri Ponzo and Don Fraser; a successful visit to see the blooming Ghost Orchid (_Dendrophylax lindenii_), which currently has one blossom and three buds. This was Val's and Don's first visit to Corkscrew and my first in several years. Val and Don were doing much butterfly and dragonfly watching, while I birded the boardwalk mostly by myself. It took four hours to reach the shortcut loop on the western side of the loop, where I joined Val and Don, but only 40 more minutes to complete the full boardwalk loop. We then relaxed in the Visitor's Center, drinking liquids and watching the feeders/bird fountain. The weather was sunny, warm, humid, with calm winds at the start, but it had become very hot and humid by the end (good thing the boardwalk is heavily shaded). Parts of the boardwalk, and many trees, were destroyed by Hurricane Irma in September 2017 and had not yet been repaired. We left at 1400 and headed back to Sarasota.

Took these photos while completing an eBird checklist. (https://ebird.org/checklist/S202962283). I think these may belong to one of the Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks that were present. Please help ID if possible!
What a lovely family, such good parents <3
